contexts.text: Because the problem definition and challenge are reconstructed from the complete target paper, theoretically they could inadvertently retain method-specific clues to the target solution if the LLM that performs this task doesn’t follow instructions well. We manually inspected the extracted problem definition and challenge for 50 randomly sampled target examples, comparing each with its source paper. We found no instances (0/50) in which the input exposed the target method, including through method-specific terminology, assumptions, examples, or problem decompositions that would reveal the solution.   E Experiment Configuration   E.1 Training and Inference Configuration   We train one LoRA adapter per role on the Qwen3.6-27B backbone with asynchronous GRPO. Each adapter uses rank 32, scaling α = 64, and no dropout, applied to all linear modules except the output projection and the visual tower, which is unused for this text-only task. Optimization uses AdamW with a constant learning rate of 5× 10−6, weight decay 0.01, no warmup, and gradient norm clipping at 1.0, in bfloat16 with tensor parallel size 8 on H100 GPUs. Each GRPO step draws 64 prompts with 8 generations per prompt, giving 512 rollouts per step, and applies two gradient updates per step at a training batch of 256 rollouts.

contexts.text: We train one LoRA adapter per role using asynchronous GRPO with a maximum policy staleness of one step and an importance sampling correction for the resulting staleness. Sequence lengths and the number of training steps are calibrated per role, and the full optimization configuration is reported in Appendix E.1.   B.2 Training Design Choices   Before settling on the final reward and environment, we explored several alternatives.   Full-text reading over metadata. We compared giving the reader the paper full text against a faster metadata- only digest. The metadata variant collapsed training, with a near-zero mean reward and most rollouts truncated at initialization, against a mean reward around 0.5 for the full-text reader, so we kept full-text reading and recovered throughput with asynchronous GRPO rather than by shortening the input.   Comparative innovator reward. We also tested a pairwise innovator reward that asks whether each candidate field is better than its reference counterpart, in place of the absolute reference-grounded score. This variant increasingly favored longer and more elaborate answers: its training reward spiked to ∼0.83, suggesting that the judge rewarded length and elaboration independently of substance, and then repeatedly collapsed. By contrast, the absolute-rubric reward remained stable around 0.66, so we kept the absolute reference-anchored rubric.   Process shaping and validity gates.

contexts.text: These works demonstrate that LLM agents can perform complex data-oriented workflows. Our work differs in its objective: the agent is not primarily collecting web data or solving data-science competitions, but acting as a data scientist whose output is training or evaluation data for another model. The core optimization target is therefore the learning value of the generated data, as measured by task-specific evaluators and solver behavior.   Self-improvement, self-play, and challenger–solver data. Autodata is also related to self-improvement and self-play methods in which models generate data, rewards, or tasks for their own training. STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) bootstraps reasoning traces by iteratively generating and training on successful rationales. Self-Rewarding Language Models (Yuan et al., 2024) use the model itself as an LLM-as-a-judge reward source during iterative preference training. More adversarial or curriculum-oriented approaches train models with self-generated tasks: Self-Challenging Language Model Agents (Zhou et al., 2025) generate tool-use tasks together with verification functions, Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025a) proposes and solves its own verifiable   13reasoning tasks without external data, and SPICE (Liu et al., 2025) uses a challenger–reasoner setup grounded in corpora.

We randomly partitioned them into 14,500 training papers, 200 validation papers, and 277 held-out test papers, and used the same partition for all three agents. Qwen3.6-27B converts each human-authored target paper into the required proposal schema, preserving the research problem, proposed method, model design, related work, and limitations, while removing all measured experimental outcomes. This results-masked representation records directions that human researchers have pursued without exposing their experimental success.   We generate training data using the extracted gaps, intuitions, and research proposal, which provides the skeleton about the research direction; supporting claims and citations must be grounded in papers read through the environment. We validate every artifact carefully before adding to the training set. Appendix D reports details of the training reference construction.   5 Experiments   5.1 Experiment Setup   We evaluate IdeaScientist-Base and IdeaScientist-Trained on Qwen3.6-27B. B. Ethics We believe that there is more agreement than it seems on the normative question of whether LLMs should be used for social science and AI training data. As we have de- tailed, proponents of LLM simulations have argued for its positive impact as an accessible and scalable data source to further social science and support training new AI systems. Most of the critiques we have seen of LLM simulations do so on empirical grounds, such as the issues of diversity and bias that we address in this position paper.
